meta.progress_note: 600 of 600 planned questions drafted - COMPLETE. Batch 1-8 = RD-001-560 (fully audited with the corrected full O(n^2) all-pairs scan). This completes question-writing; the dataset is still UNREVIEWED pending named RD clinical sign-off before any publication or model benchmarking run - see README_scoring_methodology.md and qa_report.md.
meta.domain_framework_note: These 7 domains are a working benchmark framework spanning core RD practice areas (foundational science, care process, clinical MNT, food science, foodservice management, education/counseling, and research/QI). They are broader than CDR's official 4-domain RD exam blueprint (Principles of Dietetics; Nutrition Care for Individuals/Groups; Management of Food and Nutrition Programs and Services; Foodservice Systems) and should be labeled as a custom benchmark structure, not represented as the literal CDR exam blueprint, unless a named RD reviewer explicitly maps and approves this mapping.

questions.question: Which of the following vitamins is fat-soluble and can be stored in clinically significant amounts in the liver?

options.B: Vitamin B6

questions.reference: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in liver and adipose tissue.

options.B: Thiamin (B1)

options.B: Vitamin C

questions.question: Calculate BMI for a patient who is 1.70 m tall and weighs 82 kg. Report to one decimal place.
A patient's usual body weight is 160 lb; current weight is 142 lb. Calculate % usual body weight (round to nearest whole percent).

questions.question: Explain the difference between a 'nutrition diagnosis' (as used in the Nutrition Care Process) and a medical diagnosis, and give one example of each for the same patient scenario.
rubric_points: States that a nutrition diagnosis describes a specific nutrition problem the RD can independently treat, using PES (Problem-Etiology-Signs/Symptoms) format
States that a medical diagnosis describes a disease or pathology treated by the medical team and does not change based on nutrition intervention alone
Gives a plausible matched example pair (e.g., medical dx: Type 2 diabetes; nutrition dx: excessive carbohydrate intake related to lack of nutrition-related knowledge)
Notes the nutrition diagnosis can resolve/change with intervention even if the medical diagnosis persists

questions.question: Describe the concept of protein complementation and provide one example food combination that yields a complete amino acid profile.
rubric_points: Explains that complementation combines two incomplete protein sources whose limiting amino acids offset each other
Correctly notes complementation does not need to occur in the same meal, only within the same day
Gives a valid example (e.g., rice + beans, peanut butter + whole wheat bread, hummus + pita)

questions.question: Explain the physiological difference between soluble and insoluble fiber and name one health benefit associated with each.
rubric_points: Correctly states soluble fiber dissolves/forms a gel in water; insoluble does not
Correctly links soluble fiber to a benefit such as lowering LDL cholesterol or blunting post-meal glucose rise
Correctly links insoluble fiber to a benefit such as increasing stool bulk / promoting regularity / preventing constipation

questions.question: Which validated tool is most commonly used for rapid nutrition risk screening on hospital admission?

options.B: Mini-Mental State Exam

questions.question: A PES statement is structured in which order?

options.B: Problem - Etiology - Signs/Symptoms

questions.reference: PES = 'Problem related to Etiology as evidenced by Signs/Symptoms'.

questions.question: Which biochemical marker best reflects iron stores rather than acute iron status, and is also an acute-phase reactant that can be falsely elevated with inflammation?

options.B: Serum iron

questions.question: A patient lost 8 lb over the past month. Their usual body weight is 175 lb. Calculate % weight change (round to nearest tenth of a percent) and state whether it meets the commonly cited 1-month 'severe' weight-loss threshold of >5%.
questions.reference: 8/175 x100 = 4.57% -> 4.6%; this is just below the >5% 'severe' 1-month threshold, so it does NOT meet the severe criterion (FIXED in QA pass: prior reference text incorrectly and confusingly also called this 'significant'; the RD reviewer should confirm which categorical label, if any, applies at 4.6%).

questions.question: Calculate ideal body weight (IBW) using the Hamwi method for a woman who is 5'4" tall (IBW = 100 lb for first 5 ft + 5 lb per inch over 5 ft for women).
A patient has a BMI of 42 and an ideal body weight (IBW) of 130 lb, actual weight 240 lb. Calculate adjusted body weight (AdjBW) using AdjBW = IBW + 0.25(actual weight - IBW).

Write a complete PES statement for a hospitalized patient with a new diagnosis of dysphagia who has been eating <25% of meals for 3 days due to fear of choking, with 4% unintentional weight loss in the past week.
rubric_points: Uses correct PES format (Problem related to Etiology as evidenced by Signs/Symptoms)
Problem is a valid AND-approved nutrition diagnosis term (e.g., inadequate oral intake)
Etiology correctly identifies the underlying cause (dysphagia / fear of aspiration/choking), not just restates the problem
Signs/symptoms cite the specific measurable evidence given (intake <25% x3 days, 4% weight loss in 1 week)

questions.question: Describe two nutrition-focused physical exam (NFPE) findings that would support a diagnosis of moderate protein-energy malnutrition per the AND/ASPEN characteristics, and what each finding suggests.
rubric_points: Identifies a valid NFPE finding (e.g., temporal wasting, interosseous muscle wasting, edema, orbital fat loss)
Correctly links the finding to loss of subcutaneous fat or muscle mass
Identifies a second distinct, valid finding with correct interpretation
Frames findings within the AND/ASPEN malnutrition characteristics framework (not just generic descriptions)

questions.question: Describe an appropriate monitoring and evaluation plan (indicators + timeframe) for a patient started on oral nutrition supplements for unintentional weight loss.
rubric_points: Specifies at least 2 relevant, measurable indicators (e.g., weight trend, % meal/supplement intake, labs such as prealbumin used cautiously, functional status)
Specifies a realistic reassessment timeframe (e.g., weekly weight, recheck intake at next visit/1-2 weeks)
Ties indicators back to the original PES/goal rather than listing unrelated labs

A patient's meal contains 60 g carbohydrate. Using an insulin-to-carb ratio of 1:10, calculate the mealtime insulin dose (units).
Estimate daily fluid needs for a 70 kg adult using the 1 mL/kcal method, assuming estimated energy needs of 2100 kcal/day.

questions.question: Explain what refeeding syndrome is, identify a patient population at high risk, and describe the key nutrition intervention used to prevent it.
rubric_points: Correctly describes refeeding syndrome as electrolyte/fluid shifts (esp. hypophosphatemia, also hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia) triggered by reintroducing nutrition after prolonged starvation
Identifies a valid at-risk population (e.g., chronic alcoholism, anorexia nervosa, prolonged NPO status, oncology patients with significant weight loss)
Describes prevention: starting nutrition support cautiously at a reduced calorie level and advancing slowly while monitoring/repleting electrolytes (especially phosphorus) before and during feeding

questions.question: Summarize MNT recommendations for a patient newly diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
rubric_points: Mentions consistent carbohydrate distribution across meals/snacks
Mentions individualized calorie needs supporting appropriate gestational weight gain (not weight loss)
Mentions self-monitoring of blood glucose and the goal of maintaining glucose targets to protect fetal outcomes
Mentions the role of physical activity and/or need for medication if MNT alone is insufficient

questions.question: Describe how the IDDSI (International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative) framework is used to manage a patient with dysphagia, including both food and liquid dimensions.
rubric_points: Correctly notes IDDSI provides a standardized numbered framework (0-7) spanning both food texture and liquid thickness
Notes food and liquid levels are assigned separately based on swallow study/SLP recommendation
Gives a plausible example of a level or modification (e.g., pureed diet, nectar-thick liquids, minced & moist)

options.B: Food cooked, then rapidly chilled and stored for later reheating/service

Total labor cost for the week was $9,500 and total revenue was $38,000. Calculate labor cost percentage.
A unit uses 40 cases of a canned good per week on average and wants a 1.5-week safety stock as its par level. Calculate the par level in cases.
Explain the concept of 'menu engineering' (the Stars/Plowhorses/Puzzles/Dogs matrix) and how a foodservice manager would use it to make menu decisions.

questions.question: Describe two methods a foodservice manager could use to forecast meal production volume for an upcoming week, and one risk of under-forecasting.
rubric_points: Names a valid forecasting method (e.g., historical count/usage trends, moving average, census/occupancy data for a hospital, reservation counts)

questions.question: Discuss one trade-off a foodservice director faces when deciding whether to source produce locally versus from a national distributor.
rubric_points: Identifies a genuine benefit of local sourcing (freshness, community relations/marketing, sometimes seasonality/quality)
Identifies a genuine trade-off/cost of local sourcing (higher and less stable pricing, inconsistent supply/quality, less volume reliability, more vendor management effort)

rubric_points: Response avoids arguing, lecturing, or immediately offering solutions (avoids 'righting reflex')
Response uses a genuine reflective listening statement or affirmation that acknowledges the client's frustration/ambivalence
Correctly names the OARS technique used and it matches the response given

questions.question: Describe two concrete strategies an RD can use to adapt nutrition education materials for a client with low health literacy.
rubric_points: Names a valid strategy (e.g., plain language, avoiding jargon, teach-back, pictures/visual aids, limiting to 3-5 key points, 'chunk and check')
Names a second distinct valid strategy

rubric_points: Correctly describes Preparation-stage strategy as helping set specific, small, achievable goals and an action plan for the near future
Correctly describes Maintenance-stage strategy as focused on relapse prevention, reinforcing gains, and problem-solving for high-risk situations

options.A: Rolling the change out organization-wide immediately

questions.question: A QI project tracks response rate to a new discharge nutrition survey: 68 surveys returned out of 200 distributed. Calculate the response rate as a percentage.
In a QI study, 25% of patients receiving usual care developed a complication, versus 15% of patients receiving a new nutrition protocol. Calculate the absolute risk reduction (percentage points).
questions.reference: 25% - 15% = 10 percentage points (ARR); NNT would be 1/0.10 = 10, included here as ARR only per question wording.

questions.question: A hospital foodservice QI project reduced average tray delivery time from 45 minutes to 36 minutes. Calculate the percent reduction.
Explain the key difference between a randomized controlled trial and an observational cohort study, and why this difference matters for causal inference.
rubric_points: Correctly states that in an RCT, exposure/intervention is randomly assigned by the researcher; in a cohort study it is not (naturally occurring)
Correctly explains randomization reduces confounding, allowing stronger causal claims, whereas observational studies are more vulnerable to confounding/bias

questions.question: Describe how a dietitian-led PDSA cycle might be applied to a real quality improvement problem in a clinical setting (give a plausible example for each of the 4 phases).
rubric_points: Plan: states a clear, testable change and prediction relevant to a plausible problem
Do: describes a small-scale test/pilot of the change
Study: describes comparing results to the prediction/baseline data
Act: describes a decision to adopt, adapt, or abandon based on the Study phase

questions.question: A colleague shares a nutrition news article claiming a supplement 'cures' a chronic disease, citing a single small non-peer-reviewed study. Explain how you would critically appraise this claim before advising patients, addressing study validity and applicability.
rubric_points: Raises a validity concern (e.g., small sample size, lack of peer review, no control group/randomization, potential conflicts of interest/funding source)
Raises an applicability/generalizability concern (e.g., population studied, dose/form used, outcome measured vs. real-world outcome of interest)
States an appropriate cautious conclusion (e.g., insufficient evidence to recommend, wait for replication/peer-reviewed publication) rather than either blanket endorsement or blanket dismissal

options.B: UVB

options.B: Small intestine (primarily jejunum)

questions.question: Using the general reference of 0.8 g protein/kg body weight/day for a healthy sedentary adult, calculate protein needs for a 70 kg adult (grams/day).

questions.question: Explain the concept of nitrogen balance and what a positive versus negative nitrogen balance indicates about a patient's protein status.

Correctly states positive nitrogen balance indicates net protein synthesis/anabolism (e.g., growth, pregnancy, recovery)
Correctly states negative nitrogen balance indicates net protein breakdown/catabolism (e.g., illness, trauma, starvation)

questions.question: Describe the role of bile in fat digestion and identify where it is produced and stored.
rubric_points: Correctly states bile emulsifies fat, increasing surface area for lipase action (bile is not itself an enzyme)
Correctly states bile is produced by the liver
Correctly states bile is stored/concentrated in the gallbladder and released into the duodenum

questions.question: Describe the three etiology-based categories of malnutrition in the AND/ASPEN framework (starvation-related, chronic disease-related, and acute disease/injury-related), with an example patient scenario for each.
rubric_points: Correctly describes starvation-related malnutrition (chronic starvation without inflammation, e.g., anorexia nervosa, food insecurity) with a plausible example
Correctly describes chronic disease-related malnutrition (mild-to-moderate chronic inflammation, e.g., COPD, CKD, cancer) with a plausible example

questions.question: Describe two key limitations of the 24-hour dietary recall as a nutrition assessment tool.
rubric_points: Names a valid limitation (e.g., relies on memory/recall bias, may not represent a 'usual' day, subject to social desirability/underreporting, requires trained interviewer for accuracy)

questions.question: Describe at least two criteria used (e.g., per NICE guidance) to identify a patient at high risk for refeeding syndrome before starting nutrition support.

Names a second distinct valid criterion

questions.question: For a patient with CKD stage 3-4 who is not yet on dialysis, protein intake is typically:

questions.question: Explain the nutrition management of phenylketonuria (PKU), including what must be restricted and how protein needs are otherwise met.

questions.question: Explain why sodium and potassium recommendations for chronic kidney disease patients need to be individualized based on CKD stage and dialysis status, rather than applying one blanket restriction to all CKD patients.

questions.question: How do internal validity and external validity differ, and what is an example of a study design choice that could improve one at the potential expense of the other?
rubric_points: Correctly distinguishes internal validity (confidence that the study accurately measures the true causal effect within its own sample, minimizing bias/confounding) from external validity (generalizability of the findings to other populations/settings)

Gives a plausible example of a trade-off (e.g., a highly controlled RCT with narrow inclusion criteria improves internal validity but may reduce external validity/generalizability to broader real-world populations)

questions.question: Explain the difference between prevalence and incidence, and why the distinction matters when interpreting epidemiological data.

Correctly explains why the distinction matters (e.g., prevalence is affected by both incidence and disease duration/survival, so a change in prevalence does not necessarily mean a change in new-case risk)

questions.question: Explain what positive predictive value (PPV) measures and how disease prevalence in the tested population affects it.
rubric_points: Correctly explains PPV as the probability that a person who tests positive actually has the disease (true positives / all positives)
Correctly explains that PPV rises with higher disease prevalence in the tested population and falls with lower prevalence, even when sensitivity and specificity stay constant

questions.question: Explain what convenience sampling is and why it can limit a study's external validity.
